items.title: Show HN: Mason – A lightweight Postgres read-replica, built on columnar storage
items.summary: Hi HN! TLDR: we’ve built an open-source drop-in replacement for a postgres read-replica, powered by duckdb’s columnar compute engine. It’s very fast. And it looks like postgres. So, this started out as: let’s just connect Clickhouse to our postgres dbs and throw our analytics queries at it instead. That will speed everything up. But we quickly found that 1) Clickhouse comes with quite the learning curve (engine optimisation) to make it fast (we needed something we could easily drop in to any customer’s postgres scenario), and 2) we had underestimated how different clickhouse’s SQL syntax was to postgres. Don’t get me wrong: we love Clickhouse (it’s ridiculously fast if you know what queries to expect), it just didn’t work for our ad-hoc postgres workloads. So we went searching for alternatives that were 1) more plug-and-play and 2) looked a lot more like postgres. We dismissed a bunch based on desk research alone: - pg_mooncake (seems to have stalled since data bricks bought them) - pg_duckdb (seems to offer fast queries, or fresh data, but not both - we needed both) - materialize/risingwave/readyset (like Clickhouse, they require knowing the query shapes upfront - not ideal for ad-hoc workloads) - firebolt (license makes it challenging to offer to our customers) - redshift / alloydb / etc (we wanted something cloud-provider agnostic) And we shortlisted 3: - pg_clickhouse (Postgres extension that parses SQL in Postgres and pushes the work down to ClickHouse) - cedarDB (closed-source, Postgres-compatible analytical database) - duckdb (open-source, embedded columnar analytics engine with a Postgres-like SQL dialect) We needed to know how they would perform on real postgres queries, so we took a backlog of 5,410 (hand-written) queries (chosen because they had been slow to execute against postgres) from 159 real postgres databases. We then generated synthetic data (dynamically using the schemas from those 159 databases) to fill 159 local databases so we could run the experiment. We then spun up the 3 short-listed tools locally, and ran each of the 5,410 queries against both postgres and the 3 tools, and compared the results: - pg_clickhouse (matched postgres 59.4% of the time, refused 39.9% of the queries and was “wrong” 0.8% of the time). - cedarDB (matched postgres 88.1% of the time, refused 8% of the queries and was “wrong” 3.9% of the time). - duckdb (matched postgres 84.1% of the time, refused 14.3% of the queries and was “wrong” 1.6% of the time). Matched meant they returned exactly the same result as postgres. Refused meant they returned an error message (usually telling you some syntax isn’t recognised). And “wrong” meant they didn’t return the same results as postgres. I appreciate that arguably postgres may be the one that is wrong in some cases - but for our use case, we considered postgres the golden source of truth. So, both duckdb and cedardb performed pretty well (correctly handled more than 80% of the postgres queries we threw at it), out-of-the box. But we really still wanted to try and cover that long-tail. We chose duckdb as its open-source license would allow us to easily work on the long tail to get the postgres SQL parity we wanted. So, Mason (linked above), is what we built, powered by duckdb, which now matches postgres on 96% of our 5,410 queries, plus hundreds of other queries that we added, testing it with Metabase, Grafana, Superset, DBeaver and Trevor.io. For the remaining 4%, it errors with a nice clear message telling you how to rewrite your SQL. We’d love your feedback on what we’ve built. Useful? How can we make it better? Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50630294 Points: 59 # Comments: 9

items.title: Show HN: Brickie – Deploy sandboxes in your own AWS account
items.summary: Hey HN, this is Alexander from Hatchet ( https://github.com/hatchet-dev/hatchet ). We’re releasing a new open-source project today called Brickie. Brickie lets you run sandboxes in your own cloud account, primarily targeting EKS on AWS. Sandboxes are an incredibly useful primitive for agentic applications. They serve two main functions: (1) a way for the agent to safely execute untrusted code, and (2) a durable filesystem for agents to preserve their state via snapshots. We decided to start building this after we started on a package called `@hatchet-dev/sandbox` to integrate more directly with various sandbox providers, like E2B, Daytona, Archil, and Modal. We discovered that a lot of users had a requirement to self-host their sandbox infra for part of (or all of) their stack, due to a self-host requirement for enterprises. We searched around for the easiest way for users to self-host a sandbox stack and agent-sandbox ( https://agent-sandbox.sigs.k8s.io ) was the closest thing to what we had in mind: it’s a kubernetes-sigs project implementing a Kubernetes operator which spawns sandboxes as pods on supported isolation layers like Firecracker, gVisor, and Kata Containers. We learned that many platform teams were adopting this because it's a standard k8s-based deployment model and is pretty easy to customize the isolation layer, network config, etc. However, it was missing some necessary features. brickie builds on top of the agent-sandbox project and extends it to support proper sandbox (filesystem-based) snapshots, fork, pause, and resume, all while bundling a proper orchestration and observability layer via Hatchet. Zooming out a bit, Hatchet is an orchestration engine which supports durable execution ( https://hatchet.run/blog/durable-execution ). Throughout 2026, we saw high adoption from users building agents using durable workflows as the statefulness layer and execution model. But as sandboxes became more popular, something didn’t sit right with us. Sandboxes _also_ provide a durability layer, but at the filesystem level, and it became important to disambiguate what we call session state from filesystem state . I wrote a lot more about this here: https://hatchet.run/blog/agent-statefulness . The problem with having state in multiple places is that it needs coordination, which adds complexity to your application. This was part of the motivation behind `@hatchet-dev/sandbox`: we wanted to provide an easy way to take coordinated snapshots of agent state, even when using an external sandbox provider. So when we started looking at self-hosted sandbox options, it was critical that this architecture was supported well. We decided to support this in brickie using a pretty simple snapshotting mechanism which tars and stores snapshots in an object store (S3). This is something we’re actively working to improve and make more performant. Brickie is early and in beta, we're looking for testers, contributors, and feedback on the deployment model. Thanks in advance! Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50629936 Points: 13 # Comments: 0
